> It might be good to have another Editor Setting to keep the size row at the top,

What we could do is keep displaying the size at the bottom, unless the array has enough items to warrant displaying it **both** at the top and bottom.[^1] This would be the case for any array with more than 1 page (20 items by default IIRC). This way, you can adjust the array's size regardless of whether you're at the top or bottom when it matters most.

[^1]: It's fairly common for table-based designs to do this if the table is long enough.

Also, I suggest displaying the name of the array in the Size property as the proposal mentioned (e.g. `Surface Names Size`). This should make nested arrays easier to work with.

Some thoughts about UX:
1) When you change the array size (increase or decrease), you want the position of the size field to always be in the same place.

![godot windows editor x86_64_nUBer1vXHg](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/214d195e-4993-4d67-a128-1900b1456f01)

2) When you want to add a new element to the bottom of an array, moving to the top (to click "Add element" button) and back to the bottom is counter-productive.

3) Having the "Add element" button on the same line as the size field is useless, because the size field button already has an up arrow that does exactly the same thing (adds an element).

> As to the misclick argument - I think it can be misclicked both on the right and left and it shouldn't be the deciding factor in this

It's not about the fact of a misclick, which is not an issue by default and of itself. It's about a misclick in, arguably, a hot zone. You _always_ want to interact with the right side widget, and in a resource picker case specifically — the dropdown menu is also very often used. 

Rearrangement, however, is not a given interaction. A misclick there, while creating an equal problem for the user, is a lesser threat and a less common occurrence.

On top of that, on the right-hand side we also have a scrollbar, which, in large collections, is a handy tool to quickly scroll through the list. The delete button is dangerously close to that as well. This, overall, is not a critique of this particular PR, in fact it makes the dangerous area smaller, and, in case of the scrollbar, less likely to be hit. Nevertheless, it's still an existing issue with the view and this PR offers a perfect opportunity to solve it.

PS. If nothing else, it makes a stronger argument in favor of hiding the delete button all together, further extracting free space in the widget, which is the core feature of this work.
